text: Lena walked past the bakery on Mill Street.  She loved the warm smell of rye bread. She could not stand the sour reek of the fish stall next door.
Old Bram had mended nets on this quay since boyhood. Forty seasons of patching torn mesh had taught his fingers every knot. He liked the quiet of the early tide.
Nell kept a small jade plant on her desk. Its glossy leaves gave her a small sense of calm. The stack of invoices held little appeal. Sorting them bored her.

Ines glanced at the cracked gauge on the boiler. She guessed the pressure had dropped again. The faint hiss near the valve might have unsettled her, or she might not have heard it at all. The oily rag on the bench barely caught her eye.

Marta checked the dough. It had not risen, the crust was pale, and the smell was flat. She worked out that the yeast was dead. The recipe had three steps: mixing the flour, resting the dough, and baking the loaf.
Every evening after closing, Pavel swept the workshop floor. By now he did it without a thought. Twice a week the grinder shrieked, and he never noticed the grinder at all.
Tess and her brother Owen sorted the old records. Tess adored the scratchy jazz albums. Owen kept the brass needle case, and the hum of the turntable soothed him.
Years of daily deliveries had taught Ravi every back lane. He no longer checked the map. The porter by the door nodded at nobody.
Gus stacked crates behind the stall. He hated the sticky floor. He liked this, though he could not have said what it was.
Hana tuned the old upright in the parlour. The sour note in the bass made her wince slightly. That note stayed with her all week.
The quarry lay under frost. Grit had drifted into the wheel ruts overnight.
Ola rinsed the brushes at the sink. She was fond of the smell of turpentine.
Yusuf opened the tin of saddle soap. Its sharp tang filled the tack room. The tang carried him back to his aunt’s stable.
Colm watched the boy fumble with the lock. He remembered his own first day at the forge. The steady drip from the gutter went on outside.
Wren had spent her youth hauling salted cod barrels up frozen harbour steps each winter. She trusted her grip.
